name: Senmaizuke (Kyoto thin-sliced Shogoin turnip pickle)
text: Kyoto pickle of Shogoin kabu (a Kyoto heritage turnip) sliced paper-thin, salted and layered with kombu. Treated as a delicate, short-keeping pickle rather than a long-storage one. The inventor and date are disputed: JA Kyoto names Otoh Tozaburo, Narita names Daikokuya Tozaburo, and both place it in the late Edo period (Keio era).
flavor: Sweet, soft and lightly sour, with kombu umami; crisp-tender slices.
use: Served cold as a side, an obanzai or kaiseki hashiyasume, and in winter, the season of the turnip.
craft: Sources describe the basic flow as thin slicing, salt pre-pickling, then main pickling with kombu between layers. The original method used only kombu and salt for the main pickling with lactic fermentation, whereas the modern mainstream uses a seasoning liquid. Sources disagree on whether it is fermented at all, so state which style you serve. The home-recipe ratio quoted is 1 kg turnip : 100 g sugar : 75 cc vinegar : 25 g salt, a shortcut and not the traditional method.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Senmaizuke, Kyoto

name: Suguki-zuke (Kamigamo suguki-na lactic pickle)
text: One of the three great Kyoto pickles, made from suguki-na, a turnip-type vegetable grown around Kamigamo, with salt only. Its character comes from lactic fermentation, and it is pressed with a lever-weight (tenbin-oshi) technique.
flavor: Deep, clean lactic sourness with the vegetable's own sweetness; no added seasoning.
use: Eaten as it is, or as a sour accent for rice and tea; the leaves and root are both used.
craft: Sources stress two points: only suguki-na and salt are used, and weight is applied by a lever (tenbin-oshi) rather than a plain stone. Doneness is judged by acidity, so check the fermented sourness against the guest's expectation. This is a true fermented pickle, unlike senmaizuke.

name: Shibazuke (Kyoto red shiso and eggplant pickle)
text: Kyoto pickle of chopped eggplant and red shiso. The traditional method uses salt only and lactic fermentation. Most commercial products today use a seasoning liquid for an acidic flavour instead.
flavor: Sharp acid, red shiso aroma and salt; the colour is a strong crimson.
use: Served with rice, chazuke and as a garnish; chopped into sushi rice or onigiri.
craft: Per Narita's description of the process: chop the vegetables, rub with salt, squeeze, weight and ferment. Ask a supplier whether the product is salt-fermented or liquid-seasoned, since these are different foods that share one name.

name: Saikyo-zuke (Saikyo white miso marinade)
text: Misozuke style from Kyoto using sweet white Saikyo miso as the curing bed. Fish such as sawara (Spanish mackerel) and gindara (black cod) are best known. Classified among miso pickles.
flavor: Sweet, mild miso savour on dense fish flesh.
use: Wiped of excess miso and grilled; also used for vegetables.
craft: Miso scorches easily, so a professional wipes off the bed before grilling and cooks over gentle heat. Classification detail comes from trade overview pages, not a Kyoto standard.

name: Shiroboshi umeboshi and chomi-umeboshi (salt tiers of Kishu Nanko-ume)
text: Shiroboshi is plain salt-cured, sun-dried Kishu Nanko-ume. Retail white-dried ume list 18% salt. Seasoned (chomi) umeboshi are far lower: one maker sells a usushio chomi umeboshi at 7%, shiso at 8% and honey at 6%. Overall retail salt runs from about 3% to nearly 20%.
flavor: 18% is sharply salty and sour; chomi versions are rounded and sweet.
use: Seasoning for onigiri, nerigoma and sauces (white-dried types); seasoned types as table pickles.
craft: Check the salt percentage first, because it governs keeping quality and the dosage in cooking. The Senpin Kishu umeboshi (tokusen) mark is an industry-body certification of Kishu A-grade quality, not a JAS standard. Searches did not surface any MAFF or JAS definition of umeboshi grades nor the doyo-boshi procedure, so those are left out.
src: Kishu Ume no Sato Nakata: usushio chomi umeboshi

name: Fukujinzuke (seven-vegetable soy pickle)
text: Soy-sauce pickle of seven vegetables: daikon, eggplant, uri (melon), turnip, nata-mame (sword bean), shiso seed and lotus root. Devised at a Ueno pickle shop in the Meiji period and spread nationwide as a portable pickle during the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese wars. The writer Baitei Kingo reportedly named it after the Benzaiten of Shinobazu Pond, one of the Seven Lucky Gods.
flavor: Sweet-salty soy, crunchy, with a faint spice.
use: Classic side to Japanese curry.
craft: Sources differ slightly on the shiso item (MAFF: shiso seed; other pages: shiso). Origin stories for its pairing with curry (a substitute for chutney on ships) are single-source accounts.

name: Bettarazuke (Tokyo koji-pickled daikon)
text: Daikon pre-salted to draw water, then pickled in rice koji and sugar for a gently sweet result. A koji pickle (kojizuke). One theory of the name is that the koji sticks (bettari) to the daikon.
flavor: Light sweetness, crunch, mild koji aroma.
use: Side pickle, eaten with the koji still clinging at fairs and at the table.
craft: The salting step controls the water load, and too wet a daikon dilutes the koji bed. Name origin is one of several theories given by MAFF.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Bettarazuke, Tokyo

name: Moriguchi-zuke (Moriguchi daikon in sake lees)
text: Long Moriguchi daikon is first salted, then packed in sake lees, and finally seasoned in mirin lees with sugar. Fuso town in Aichi sits on the Kiso River bank, whose soil suits the crop, and holds about 70% of national output.
flavor: Dense and chewy, sweet-savoury sake-lees depth.
use: Sliced thin as a sake accompaniment or with rice.
craft: A three-stage pickle: salt, sake lees, then mirin lees plus sugar. Slice thin across the grain to judge chew.

name: Miike takana-zuke (Fukuoka)
text: Takana mustard greens of Miike, salted and fermented. Counted as one of the three great na-zuke along with Nozawana and Hiroshimana.
flavor: Pungent mustard bite, sour and salty when well fermented.
use: Table pickle, filling for onigiri, in fried rice and as ramen topping.
craft: A fermented, not fresh, pickle: judge sourness and pungency. Cooking uses are standard practice and not drawn from the cited page.

name: Aso takana-zuke (Kumamoto)
text: Traditional takana pickle of Aso city. The MAFF page lists three ingredients: takana, salt and chili.
flavor: Sharp mustard heat with a chili edge, salty-sour.
use: Eaten with rice and tea; also stir-fried or in rice dishes.
craft: Three-ingredient pickle, so quality depends on the greens, the salt balance and the fermentation. The Aso origin and local method are given on the MAFF page.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Aso takanazuke, Kumamoto

name: Tottori sakyu rakkyo-zuke (dune rakkyo)
text: Rakkyo grown on Tottori's dune sand, cultivated since the Edo period. Salt-pickling and seasoning processing began around Showa 40, stabilising prices. Honzuke: wash, salt for at least 2 weeks, desalt, then pickle; sweet vinegar (amazu) is the most common.
flavor: Crisp, pungent, sharply sweet-sour.
use: Accompaniment for curry and rice; the pickled bulb is eaten whole or sliced.
craft: Harvest is late May to mid June per MAFF; another source says mid May start, market late May for about a month. JA Zen-noh Tottori advises pickling early to mid June bulbs, which are ripe enough to keep long.
src: MAFF Uchi no kyodo ryori: Rakkyozuke, Tottori
JA Zen-noh Tottori: how to pickle rakkyo

name: Shima-rakkyo (Okinawan small rakkyo)
text: Okinawan variety, smaller and more strongly flavoured than mainland rakkyo. Eaten as tempura, amazu-zuke or quick salt pickle. Main growing areas: north of the main island, Miyako and Iejima.
flavor: Strong, pungent, garlicky crunch.
use: Salt-rubbed with a day or two in the fridge, tempura, awamori accompaniment.
craft: Quick salting: rub raw bulbs with salt and chill for 1 to 2 days. One page gives January to May as harvest, from a single source of uncertain reliability; confirm locally.

name: Katsuo shuto (bonito viscera salt-cure)
text: Salt-cured, matured viscera from katsuobushi processing, mainly stomach and intestine with pyloric caeca. Per Wikipedia, 30% salt on raw weight is mixed in, sealed and matured at least 3 months. Name means sake thief.
flavor: Intensely salty, deep umami, fish-gut richness.
use: A small amount on the tongue with sake; as a seasoning in cooked dishes.
craft: 30% salt gives long keeping, so dose by the grain. Associated with Kochi bonito culture but the cited sources do not state its origin outright.

name: Konowata and kuchiko (sea-cucumber intestine and gonad)
text: Konowata is the sea cucumber's intestine, salted and matured; one of the three great Japanese delicacies. Noto was the old source, and Owari and Mikawa sent it to the Tokugawa shogun in the Edo period. Kuchiko is made from the gonad; very lightly salted 'nama-kuchiko' is sold.
flavor: Briny, marine and sticky; kuchiko richer and more concentrated.
use: A small portion with sake in winter, the main season.
craft: Check salt level and freshness; sources are Wikipedia and retail pages.

name: Daitokuji natto (temple shiokara natto)
text: Shiokara natto made by koji fermentation, not Bacillus subtilis. Descends from the salted soybean shi (kuki) preparation and was made at temples, hence the name tera-natto. Original form came from China, brought back by monks who travelled to Song-dynasty China.
flavor: Dry, salty-umami, miso-like, not sticky.
use: Tea-ceremony accompaniment, in cooking as a salty seasoning.
craft: Classed in Japan by koji process (shiokara natto) versus ito-hiki natto; do not mix up the two.
src: Honke Isoda: origin of Daitokuji natto

name: Hama-natto (Hamamatsu shiokara natto)
text: Specialty of Hamamatsu in Shizuoka. A shiokara natto, completely unlike ito-hiki. J-STAGE source: by process it falls into the mame-miso category, and the soybean shape stays intact.
flavor: Salty, dense, like dry soy-miso beans.
use: A rice accompaniment, tea snack and sake appetiser.
craft: Judge as a mame-miso family product, not a sticky natto.

name: Itohiki-natto vs shiokara-natto
text: Natto has two kinds: ito-hiki (sticky, the usual meaning) and shiokara natto such as Daitokuji and Hama natto, which use koji mould. A widely told legend credits Minamoto no Yoshiie (Hachimantaro) in the Gosannen War, with horse-feed beans turning into natto, centred on Tohoku. It is a legend, unproven.
flavor: Ito-hiki sticky; shiokara dry and salty.
use: Use to specify which natto is meant.
craft: Sources note Minamoto no Yoshiie origin is speculative.

name: Muro (natto fermentation room)
text: Controlled-temperature, humidity room for natto. National Natto Co-operative says fermentation ends within about 20 to 22 hours from start. Other pages cite 16 to 18 hours. Home guidance gives 35 to 40 C best, around 40 C for 18 to 24 hours.
flavor: Production term.
use: Beans steamed, spore-inoculated, packed, then held.
craft: Container insulation affects fermentation: paper cups, bags and kyogi hold heat worse than polystyrene, so adjust room temperature and humidity. Above 60 C the culture fails.
src: National Natto Cooperative: how natto is made

name: Warazuto natto (straw-wrapped natto)
text: From about 1873 (Meiji 6) natto packed in straw wrappers was sold; a source says it was cheaper and tastier than the earlier basket (zaru) natto.
flavor: Straw fragrance.
use: Traditional pack, today also a gift form.
craft: Straw carries the natto-kin; cited from one source only.

name: Nukadoko (rice-bran bed) care
text: A lactic-acid fermented bed, with yeast contributing sourness and flavour. Mix to the bottom: summer morning, noon and night; winter at least twice. Top up with bran plus salt at 5 to 7% of the bran. Optimum temperature 15 to 25 C.
flavor: Sour, yeasty, nutty.
use: Vegetable curing, nuka-zuke.
craft: If refrigerating, return to room temperature at times. About 5% salt of the bed is called palatable by one specialist.

name: Takuan-zuke drying and salt scale
text: Sun-dried daikon in salt-rice-bran. Salt depends on storage: until March, dry until the daikon bends into a he shape, 3 to 5% salt; through summer, bend to a tsu shape, about 8%. Formerly 6 to 10%; today lower.
flavor: Crisp, sweet-sour.
use: Side pickle, rice accompaniment.
craft: Mould control: reduce air exposure, raise salt, lower temperature, mist with shochu. Home and trade pages, not official standards.

name: Ika no shiokara (salted squid) salt and aging
text: Squid flesh with liver. Liver is salted firmly to drain and thicken. Salt guide: 6 g on liver per 100 g of flesh. Edible from day 3; finish within about a week, or 2 weeks for a richer taste. Freeze in portions.
flavor: Salty, liver-rich umami.
use: Sake appetiser, rice accompaniment.
craft: Weak liver salt gives a watery result; do not dip tasting chopsticks into the tub.

name: Tsukemono classification by medium
text: MAFF splits pickles into those where microbes act directly and secondary fermented types using koji, miso, soy sauce, sake lees or bran, plus non-fermented asazuke and seasoned pickles. By medium: shiozuke, nukazuke, kasuzuke, suzuke, kojizuke, misozuke, shoyuzuke.
flavor: Classification term.
use: Specifying pickle method.
craft: Kasuzuke uses sake or mirin lees (Narazuke, wasabi-zuke); some pickles can be classed differently by medium.
